title: Worship and Life in the Land

date.label: Undated Deuteronomic discourse and legislation
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: Deut 12:1 — “These are the statutes and judgments, which ye shall observe to do in the land, which the LORD God of thy fathers giveth thee to possess it.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 12:1, read in full (BibleGateway).

claims.claim: Deut 12:2–3 commands the destruction of all Canaanite cult places — “upon the high mountains, and upon the hills, and under every green tree” — overthrowing altars, breaking pillars, burning groves, hewing down graven images.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 12:2–3, read in full; JFB on Deut 12:2 (the “places” as consecrated enclosures, not temples).

claims.claim: The chosen-place formula — “the place which the LORD your God shall choose out of all your tribes to put his name there” — is repeated through Deut 12–16, and the place is never named in Deuteronomy.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 12:5, 11, 14, 18, 21, 26; 14:23–25; 15:20; 16:2, 6, 7, 11, 15, 16, read in full; JFB on Deut 12:5 (“in all the references made to it by Moses, the name is never mentioned”).

claims.claim: Deut 12:5–7, 11–12 — burnt offerings, sacrifices, tithes, heave offerings, vows, freewill offerings, and firstlings are all brought to the chosen place, where Israel eats and rejoices before the LORD with sons, daughters, servants, and the Levite.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 12:5–7, 11–12, read in full.

claims.claim: Deut 12:8 — “Ye shall not do after all the things that we do here this day, every man whatsoever is right in his own eyes.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 12:8, read in full.

claims.claim: Deut 12:13–14 — “Take heed to thyself that thou offer not thy burnt offerings in every place that thou seest: but in the place which the LORD shall choose in one of thy tribes, there thou shalt offer thy burnt offerings.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 12:13–14, read in full; Richelle (read in full) quotes vv. 13–14 as the clearest statement of the centralization demand.

claims.claim: Deut 12:15–16, 20–25 permits secular slaughter and meat-eating “in all thy gates,” clean and unclean alike, as of the roebuck and the hart — but forbids eating blood: “for the blood is the life; and thou mayest not eat the life with the flesh” (v. 23); blood is poured “upon the earth as water.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 12:15–16, 20–25, read in full; JFB on Deut 12:15–16 (the wilderness tabernacle rule dispensed with on settlement).

claims.claim: Deut 12:17–19, 26–27 — tithes, vows, and holy things must be eaten before the LORD at the chosen place, not within the gates; “take heed to thyself that thou forsake not the Levite as long as thou livest upon the earth.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 12:17–19, 26–27, read in full; JFB on Deut 12:26 (the “extraordinary tithes or gifts” carried as peace offerings).

claims.claim: Deut 12:29–31 warns Israel not to be “snared by following” the dispossessed nations or to enquire after their gods, naming as their abomination that “even their sons and their daughters they have burnt in the fire to their gods.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 12:29–31, read in full; JFB on Deut 12:29–30 (the “local deities” fear behind the warning).

claims.claim: Deut 12:32 — “What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 12:32, read in full.

claims.claim: Deut 12 requires sacrifice at one chosen sanctuary (the majority reading); Greenspahn’s generic-article reading, that the syntax does not require limitation to a single place, has met with little approval.
claims.evidence: Richelle (read in full) on Greenspahn vs Arnold; Arnold, VT 64 (2014) 236–248, and Greenspahn, VT 64 (2014) 227–235 — both abstract/search excerpt only, NOT verified for detailed arguments, so this claim is capped at Probable and rests on Richelle’s summary.

claims.claim: Tel Moza: a monumental Iron II temple stood ~7 km northwest of Jerusalem from the late 10th/early 9th century BCE until the early 6th century BCE — in antis plan (62 × 43 ft), with an unhewn-stone altar, a refuse pit of sheep/goat bones, an offering podium, figurines, and a decorated cult stand — on the site of a royal granary.
claims.evidence: Kisilevitz & Lipschits, “Another Temple in Judah!” BAR 46.1 (2020), read in full.

claims.claim: Tel Arad: a Judahite fortress temple was in use in the 8th century BCE and was deliberately decommissioned (buried under earth; standing stones laid aside; incense altars plastered over) in the late 8th century BCE, and no cult structure was erected there when the fortress was rebuilt in the 7th century.
claims.evidence: Herzog (Arad/Beersheba) not read directly — second-hand via Richelle (read in full) and Kleiman (footnotes/summary read); Aharoni’s two-stage (Hezekiah + Josiah) reading is shown chimerical by Herzog’s analysis (Kleiman n. 16). Capped at Probable.

claims.claim: Arad and Tel Moza are evidence of cultic DIVERSITY, not direct proof of the historicity or date of a particular reform, nor proof of the complete meaning of Deut 12.
claims.evidence: Shared record §§7–8 (Richelle, read in full; Kisilevitz & Lipschits, read in full); Phase 2 Correction Record; Scholarly Disagreement Register #4.

claims.claim: The historicity of Hezekiah’s reform (2 Kgs 18:4, 22 — two verses, possibly interpolated) and of Josiah’s reform (2 Kgs 22–23 — literarily massive, archaeologically almost unattested) is debated; historians range from both-ahistorical to both-historical.
claims.evidence: Richelle (read in full), §§4–6 and Conclusion.

claims.claim: A de facto centralization is a live alternative: Sennacherib’s 701 BCE invasion destroyed many countryside cult places while sparing Jerusalem, and religious leaders may have read this as a sign YHWH had chosen Jerusalem — with Hezekiah possibly finishing what Sennacherib began.
claims.evidence: Richelle (read in full), §5; Edelman, Fried, Na’aman as cited therein (second-hand).

claims.claim: Deut 12 concerns animal sacrifice specifically, not every kind of religious ritual: when the Elephantine priests (late 5th century BCE) sought to rebuild their YHWH temple, the governors permitted vegetal and incense offerings while avoiding any mention of holocausts.
claims.evidence: Richelle (read in full), §2, citing Granerød; the Elephantine letters themselves were not read directly.

claims.claim: Deut 13:1–5 — a prophet or dreamer of dreams whose sign or wonder comes to pass, but who says “let us go after other gods,” is not to be hearkened to, and “shall be put to death”; the test is the message, not the miracle — “for the LORD your God proveth you.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 13:1–5, read in full; JFB on Deut 13:1 (no prodigy “should be allowed to shake their belief”).

claims.claim: Deut 13:6–11 — the secret enticer, even a brother, son, daughter, wife, or closest friend, is to receive no consent, pity, sparing, or concealment; the accuser’s hand is first, then the people’s, and the enticer is stoned, “and all Israel shall hear, and fear.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 13:6–11, read in full; JFB on Deut 13:6, 9 (accusation before a magistrate; trial and conviction, not private killing).

claims.claim: Deut 13:12–18 — an apostate city is dealt with only after diligent inquiry (“enquire, and make search, and ask diligently”); if the report is true, its inhabitants are smitten, the city and all its spoil burned, “it shall be an heap for ever; it shall not be built again,” and “there shall cleave nought of the cursed thing to thine hand.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 13:12–18, read in full; JFB on Deut 13:14–17 (idolatry as treason; no spoil taken).

claims.claim: There is no known archaeological or historical attestation of a Deut 13 apostate-city destruction.
claims.evidence: Stated as an absence: no excavated Israelite city is tied to the Deut 13 procedure in any source read for this dossier (Richelle’s survey lists no such case).

claims.claim: Deut 14:1–2 — “Ye are the children of the LORD your God: ye shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead. For thou art an holy people… a peculiar people unto himself, above all the nations.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 14:1–2, read in full.

claims.claim: Deut 14:3–8 — the land-animal rule: any beast “that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud” may be eaten (ox, sheep, goat, hart, roebuck, fallow deer, wild goat, pygarg, wild ox, chamois); the camel, hare, and coney (cud, no divided hoof) and the swine (divided hoof, no cud) are unclean, flesh not eaten, carcass not touched.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 14:3–8, read in full (BibleGateway KJV text).

claims.claim: Deut 14:9–10 — of water creatures, “all that have fins and scales shall ye eat”; whatever has not fins and scales “ye may not eat; it is unclean unto you.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 14:9–10, read in full.

claims.claim: Deut 14:11–20 — all clean birds may be eaten; twenty named birds (eagle, ossifrage, ospray, glede, kite, vulture, raven, owl, night hawk, cuckow, hawk, little owl, great owl, swan, pelican, gier eagle, cormorant, stork, heron, lapwing, bat) may not; “every creeping thing that flieth is unclean.” Some species identifications are uncertain in modern scholarship.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 14:11–20, read in full; the identification uncertainty is noted in modern translations (BibleGateway CEB note: “the species of many of the birds in 14:12–18 is uncertain” — search excerpt only).

claims.claim: Deut 14:21 — “Ye shall not eat of anything that dieth of itself”: it may be given to the stranger within the gates or sold to an alien; “thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother’s milk.” The rationale for the kid prohibition is not stated in the text.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 14:21, read in full. The prohibition occurs three times in identical words (Ex 23:19; 34:26; Deut 14:21).

claims.claim: The rationale of “seethe a kid in his mother’s milk” is debated: the Ugaritic fertility-rite reading (KTU 1.23, a kid boiled in its mother’s milk as a fertility rite) versus Mealy’s figure-of-speech proposal (a peasant rent-tactic, keyed to the firstfruits context).
claims.evidence: Mealy, Biblical Interpretation 20 (2012) 35–72, abstract/search excerpt only; Milgrom’s Ugaritic account, search excerpt only; KTU 1.23 reading itself disputed. NOT verified for detailed arguments.

claims.claim: Deut 14:22–27 — the annual tithe of corn, wine, oil, and firstlings is eaten “before the LORD thy God, in the place which he shall choose… that thou mayest learn to fear the LORD thy God always”; if the way is too long it may be turned into money and spent there “for whatsoever thy soul lusteth after”; the Levite within the gates is not to be forsaken.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 14:22–27, read in full.

claims.claim: Deut 14:28–29 — at the end of three years the whole tithe of that year’s increase is laid up within the gates, and “the Levite, (because he hath no part nor inheritance with thee,) and the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow… shall come, and shall eat and be satisfied.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 14:28–29, read in full.

claims.claim: Deut 15:1–6 — “At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release”: every creditor releases what a neighbour/brother owes, “because it is called the LORD’s release”; of a foreigner it may be exacted again; “there shall be no poor among you” if Israel obeys, and Israel “shalt lend unto many nations, but thou shalt not borrow.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 15:1–6, read in full.

claims.claim: Whether the seventh-year release is an absolute remission of debts or a temporary suspension of exaction for that year is debated.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 15:2 (read in full: “not by an absolute discharge… but by passing over that year without exacting payment”) vs. the Encyclopedia article (read in part: debts “are to be remitted”) and most modern readings.

claims.claim: Deut 15:7–11 — the poor brother is not to meet a hardened heart or a shut hand; the lender must “open thine hand wide” and lend “sufficient for his need”; beware the thought “the seventh year, the year of release, is at hand” as a reason to give nothing; “for the poor shall never cease out of the land.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 15:7–11, read in full; JFB on Deut 15:7–11 (the warning against letting the release law prevent lending).

claims.claim: Deut 15:12–18 — a Hebrew man or woman sold into service serves six years and goes free in the seventh, “thou shalt not let him go away empty” but “furnish him liberally out of thy flock, and out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress”; the servant who loves his master may stay, his ear bored with an awl unto the door, “thy servant for ever”; “he hath been worth a double hired servant to thee.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 15:12–18, read in full; JFB on Deut 15:12–18 (the departure gift as provision to regain status; the exodus memory as motive).

claims.claim: Mesopotamian royal mīšarum/andurārum edicts are the closest ancient Near Eastern parallel to Deut 15’s release: Old Babylonian kings issued periodic remissions of debts and releases of debt-bondage (extant exemplar: Ammi-ṣaduqa, 17th century BCE), but as irregular royal acts, not as a fixed septennial divine law.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia article (Greenberg), “Sabbatical Year and Jubilee,” ANE legal background section, read in part (lines 105–138); the Ammi-ṣaduqa edict itself was not read directly.

claims.claim: Deut 15:19–23 — all firstling males of herd and flock are sanctified to the LORD, never worked or shorn, and eaten “before the LORD thy God year by year in the place which the LORD shall choose”; a blemished firstling is not sacrificed but may be eaten within the gates like the roebuck and the hart; “only thou shalt not eat the blood thereof.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 15:19–23, read in full; JFB on Deut 15:19 (the second firstlings; cf. Deut 12:17–18; 14:23).

claims.claim: The seventh-year release has no pre-exilic attestation outside the law texts; the post-exilic community agreed to forgo debts in the sabbatical year (Neh 10:31), and the sabbatical year was observed in the Second Temple period (1 Macc 6:49, 53; Josephus, Ant. 14:475), while the Jubilee was not.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia article (read in part: biblical section lines 6–29 and post-biblical section lines 142–230); Neh 10:31, 1 Macc, and Josephus cited therein, not read directly.

claims.claim: Deut 16:1–8 — Passover is kept in the month of Abib, sacrificed “in the place which the LORD shall choose,” not “within any of thy gates,” at evening, “at the going down of the sun”; seven days of unleavened bread, “the bread of affliction,” with no leaven seen in all the coast; the seventh day a solemn assembly with no work.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 16:1–8, read in full; Bible Odyssey, “Feasts, Festivals, and Fasts” (read in full) on the dates.

claims.claim: Deut 16:9–12 — the Feast of Weeks is kept seven weeks from putting the sickle to the corn, with a freewill offering “according as the LORD thy God hath blessed thee,” and rejoicing before the LORD with household, servants, Levite, stranger, fatherless, and widow, remembering slavery in Egypt.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 16:9–12, read in full; Bible Odyssey (read in full) on the seven-week count.

claims.claim: Deut 16:13–15 — the Feast of Tabernacles is kept seven days after gathering “thy corn and thy wine,” with rejoicing of the same household and landless company, “in the place which the LORD shall choose,” because the LORD blesses “all thine increase, and… all the works of thine hands.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 16:13–15, read in full; Bible Odyssey (read in full) on the seventh-month ingathering.

claims.claim: Deut 16:16–17 — “Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the LORD thy God in the place which he shall choose; in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles: and they shall not appear before the LORD empty: every man shall give as he is able.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 16:16–17, read in full.

claims.claim: The three feasts join the agricultural year to the memory of redemption, and Deuteronomy’s distinctive emphasis is inclusive rejoicing: the feasts gather the whole household plus the Levite, stranger, fatherless, and widow at the chosen place.
claims.evidence: Bible Odyssey (read in full); BiblicalTraining, “Festivals” (search excerpt only — corroboration, not sole basis).

claims.claim: The chosen place is Jerusalem in Kings’ reading (1 Kgs 8; 2 Kgs 23) and Gerizim in the Samaritan reading, but Deuteronomy itself never names it; the MT of 1 Kgs 8:16 does not name Jerusalem, while 2 Chr 6:5–6 does, and 4Q54 attests the Jerusalem reading.
claims.evidence: Richelle (read in full), §2 (1 Kgs 8:16 / 2 Chr 6:5–6 / 4Q54); the MT, Chronicles, and 4Q54 texts themselves were not collated directly.

claims.claim: Prescribed worship and attested practice diverge: the law prescribes one sanctuary, while archaeology attests many sanctuaries operating simultaneously in monarchic Judah. The two must be presented as separate questions, not collapsed into each other.
claims.evidence: Synthesis of clm-deu-04-012/013/014; Richelle (read in full); Kisilevitz & Lipschits (read in full).

connections.note: The same command — destroy altars, break pillars, burn groves — given in Deut 7:5 and restated in Deut 12:2–3.

Solomon’s prayer: “that thine eyes may be open toward this house night and day, even toward the place of which thou hast said, My name shall be there” — Kings identifies the chosen place as Jerusalem.
Josiah “brought all the priests from the towns of Judah [to Jerusalem] and defiled the shrines… from Geba to Beersheba” — the reform enacting Deut 12’s centralization.
The blood prohibition in both: blood is not to be eaten; Lev 17:11 gives the rationale (“the life of the flesh is in the blood”).
“For the blood is the life” (Deut 12:23) // “the life of the flesh is in the blood” (Lev 17:11).
Jeremiah condemns the burning of sons and daughters in the valley of Hinnom — “which I commanded them not, neither came it into my heart” — the abomination Deut 12:31 names.
Israel “caused their sons and their daughters to pass through the fire” — the practice Deut 12:31 forbids, as Kings narrates it.
The two false-prophet tests: Deut 13 (the message, even with a fulfilled sign) and Deut 18 (the word that does not come to pass).
“There shall arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders” — the same test as Deut 13:1–3: wonders do not validate the message.
“Believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” — the New Testament form of Deut 13’s test.
“He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” — the same conflict of kinship and loyalty, resolved in the opposite direction by grace rather than by stoning.
Achan and all that he had are destroyed for the devoted thing, and a heap is raised — the same ḥerem logic applied to a person within Israel.
The same land-animal rule (divided hoof + cud) and the same four exceptions.
The same fish rule (fins and scales).
The same forbidden birds and flying creeping things, in parallel lists.
“Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother’s milk” — identical words.
“Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother’s milk” — identical words (third occurrence).
The tithe given to the Levites “because they have no part nor inheritance” — the institution behind Deut 14:27.
The third-year tithe for the Levite, stranger, fatherless, and widow, confessed in Deut 26:12–13.
The post-exilic community’s agreement to forgo debts in the seventh year — the release observed in history.
“At the end of seven years let ye go every man his brother an Hebrew” — Jeremiah cites the release law against Zedekiah’s Jerusalem.
“For ye have the poor always with you” — Jesus quotes Deut 15:11 (“the poor shall never cease out of the land”).
The Hebrew servant’s six years and the ear-piercing rite, restated with the departure gift and the exodus motive.
Zedekiah proclaims a release of Hebrew servants and the people renege — the Deut 15 law invoked and broken in history.
“Sanctify unto me all the firstborn” — the firstling law of Deut 15:19 in its Exodus form.
The firstling of ox, sheep, or goat “thou shalt not redeem… the flesh shall be thine” — the priestly disposition of the firstlings.
The Passover institution — the lamb, the night, the haste — which Deut 16:1–8 relocates to the chosen place.
Josiah keeps the Passover in Jerusalem “as it is written in the book of this covenant” — the centralized Passover of Deut 16.
The seven-week count and the Feast of Weeks, in parallel form.
“When the day of Pentecost was fully come” — the fiftieth day after Passover, the Feast of Weeks fulfilled at Pentecost.
The Feast of Tabernacles, seven days, after the ingathering, in parallel form.
“Now the Jew’s feast of tabernacles was at hand” — Jesus goes up to the feast in Jerusalem.
“In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried… If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink” — spoken at Tabernacles.
“Three times thou shalt keep a feast unto me in the year” — the three pilgrim feasts in their Exodus form.
Jesus’ parents “went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover” — the pilgrim rule of Deut 16:16 kept in the Gospels.
“For the LORD hath chosen Zion; he hath desired it for his habitation. This is my rest for ever” — the chosen-place language applied to Zion.
